Endogeneity: IV, Hausman-Taylor, GMM and selection

Source: vignettes/panglm-endogeneity.Rmd
panglm-endogeneity.Rmd

Fixed effects remove confounding by stable individual traits. They do not help when a regressor responds to time-varying shocks, when the regressor of interest does not vary over time, when the model contains the lagged outcome, or when the outcome is missing for reasons related to the outcome itself. This vignette covers the four tools panglm offers for these cases:

Problem Example Tool
Time-varying regressor correlated with the error insurance chosen after a health shock paniv(), fixed-effects 2SLS
Time-invariant regressor correlated with the individual effect schooling and frailty paniv(model = "hausmantaylor")
Lagged outcome, state dependence habit persistence in smoking pangmm(), Arellano-Bond and Blundell-Bond
Outcome observed only for a selected subsample questionnaire non-response panselect(), Wooldridge (1995) correction

The data are simulated with known true values so that the bias of the naive estimators is visible. The samples are small to keep the build fast; the companion book uses larger panels and more bootstrap replicates.

library(panglm)

Instrumental variables with fixed effects

Patients buy private insurance after a health shock (need) that also raises their doctor visits, so insurance is correlated with the time-varying error and the within estimator is biased. An employer offer of insurance shifts coverage but has no direct effect on visits, so it is a valid instrument. The true effect of insurance is 0.6.

set.seed(1)
N <- 300; TT <- 4
d <- data.frame(id = rep(seq_len(N), each = TT), wave = rep(seq_len(TT), N))
alpha <- rep(rnorm(N), each = TT)      # unobserved frailty
s0 <- rep(rnorm(N), each = TT)         # family background
need <- rnorm(N * TT)                  # time-varying health shock
d$school <- round(12 + 2 * s0 + alpha)
d$female <- rep(rbinom(N, 1, 0.5), each = TT)
d$offer <- rbinom(N * TT, 1, plogis(s0))
d$income <- rnorm(N * TT) + 0.5 * alpha
d$insured <- as.numeric(d$offer + need + rnorm(N * TT) > 0.5)
d$visits <- 1 + 0.6 * d$insured + 0.2 * d$income + alpha + need +
  rnorm(N * TT)

The formula y ~ regressors | instruments follows plm: exogenous regressors appear on both sides, and a regressor absent from the instrument list is endogenous.

coef(panglm(visits ~ insured + income, data = d, index = c("id", "wave"),
            model = "within"))
#>   insured    income 
#> 1.7440674 0.2072374
fe2sls <- paniv(visits ~ insured + income | offer + income, data = d,
                index = c("id", "wave"), model = "within", vcov = "cluster")
summary(fe2sls)
#> 
#> Call:
#> paniv(formula = visits ~ insured + income | offer + income, data = d, 
#>     index = c("id", "wave"), model = "within", vcov = "cluster")
#> 
#> Estimator: fixed-effects 2SLS 
#> N = 1200  groups = 300  vcov: cluster 
#> Endogenous: insured 
#> Excluded instruments: offer 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>         Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> insured   0.9011     0.3470   2.597  0.00942 ** 
#> income    0.2100     0.0440   4.773 1.82e-06 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> First stage (excluded instruments):
#>         partial.R2     F df1 df2   p.value F.robust  p.robust
#> insured    0.06976 67.34   1 898 7.882e-16    68.02 5.188e-15
#> Residual df: 898

The within estimator gives 1.74, nearly three times the true effect. Fixed-effects 2SLS gives 0.90 with a standard error of 0.35, so the confidence interval covers 0.6. The first-stage F statistic (68, also in its cluster-robust form) is far above the usual threshold of 10, so the instrument is strong. IV estimates are much less precise than the biased ones: that is the price of consistency. model = "random" gives the random-effects 2SLS estimator (G2SLS of Balestra and Varadharajan-Krishnakumar 1987, or EC2SLS of Baltagi 1981 with inst.method = "baltagi").

Hausman-Taylor

The effect of a time-invariant regressor such as schooling cannot be estimated with fixed effects, and random effects is biased when schooling is correlated with the individual effect. The Hausman and Taylor (1981) estimator uses the exogenous time-varying regressors twice, as their deviations from the individual means and as the means themselves, which instrument the endogenous time-invariant regressors. It needs at least as many exogenous time-varying regressors as endogenous time-invariant ones.

The formula lists all regressors, then the exogenous ones (those uncorrelated with the individual effect), as in plm::pht(). Here income and school are endogenous. True values: offer 0.4, income 0.2, female 0.3, school 0.1.

d$cost <- 2 + 0.4 * d$offer + 0.2 * d$income + 0.3 * d$female +
  0.1 * d$school + alpha + rnorm(N * TT)
ht <- paniv(cost ~ offer + income + female + school | offer + female,
            data = d, index = c("id", "wave"), model = "hausmantaylor")
summary(ht)
#> 
#> Call:
#> paniv(formula = cost ~ offer + income + female + school | offer + 
#>     female, data = d, index = c("id", "wave"), model = "hausmantaylor")
#> 
#> Estimator: Hausman-Taylor 
#> N = 1200  groups = 300  vcov: classical 
#> Exogenous time-varying:   offer 
#> Endogenous time-varying:  income 
#> Exogenous time-invariant: female 
#> Endogenous time-invariant: school 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)  2.82589    0.61620   4.586 4.52e-06 ***
#> offer        0.51550    0.07348   7.015 2.30e-12 ***
#> income       0.23628    0.03175   7.441 1.00e-13 ***
#> female       0.20763    0.13677   1.518    0.129    
#> school       0.03022    0.05156   0.586    0.558    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Variance components: idiosyncratic = 0.9913, individual = 1.147
#> theta: 0.5785 
#> Residual df: 1195
coef(panglm(cost ~ offer + income + female + school, data = d,
            index = c("id", "wave"), model = "random"))
#> (Intercept)       offer      income      female      school 
#>  0.06459459  0.31877956  0.37641975  0.21090927  0.26723300

Random effects attributes part of the frailty to schooling (0.27 against a true 0.1); Hausman-Taylor removes that bias (0.03, standard error 0.05). Its estimate is imprecise because the only excluded instrument for schooling is the mean of the employer offer. The Hausman-Taylor estimate is only as good as the exogeneity assumptions in the second part of the formula, which deserve a substantive justification.

Dynamic panels: difference and system GMM

When last period’s outcome enters the model, as with habit persistence in smoking, the lagged outcome is correlated with the individual effect (pooled OLS overstates persistence) and, after the within transformation, with the demeaned error (fixed effects understates it, Nickell 1981). GMM estimators use deeper lags of the outcome as instruments: difference GMM (Arellano and Bond 1991) for the model in first differences, system GMM (Blundell and Bond 1998) adds the model in levels with lagged differences as instruments.

The true persistence is 0.5 and the price effect is -0.3.

set.seed(1)
N <- 300; TT <- 7
g <- data.frame(id = rep(seq_len(N), each = TT), wave = rep(seq_len(TT), N))
propensity <- rnorm(N)
g$price <- rnorm(N * TT)
g$cigs <- NA
for (i in seq_len(N)) {
  r <- (i - 1) * TT + seq_len(TT)
  y <- propensity[i] / 0.5 + rnorm(1)
  for (t in seq_len(TT)) {
    y <- 0.5 * y - 0.3 * g$price[r[t]] + propensity[i] + rnorm(1)
    g$cigs[r[t]] <- y
  }
}

The formula follows plm::pgmm(): regressors, then GMM-style instruments. lag(cigs, 2:99) uses all available lags from the second on.

ab <- pangmm(cigs ~ lag(cigs, 1) + price | lag(cigs, 2:99), data = g,
             index = c("id", "wave"), model = "twostep")
summary(ab)
#> 
#> Call:
#> pangmm(formula = cigs ~ lag(cigs, 1) + price | lag(cigs, 2:99), 
#>     data = g, index = c("id", "wave"), model = "twostep")
#> 
#> Estimator: two-way two-step difference GMM (Arellano-Bond) 
#> N = 300  T = 7  equations used = 1500  instruments = 21  vcov: robust (Windmeijer) 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> lag(cigs, 1)  0.55025    0.04883  11.268   <2e-16 ***
#> price        -0.27276    0.03055  -8.927   <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Arellano-Bond AR(1) test: z = -10.24, p = < 2.2e-16
#> Arellano-Bond AR(2) test: z = -0.9451, p = 0.3446
#> Sargan test (not robust): chi2(14) = 7.391, p = 0.9186
#> Hansen J test (robust): chi2(14) = 6.259, p = 0.9595
#> Wald test for coefficients: chi2(2) = 194.5, p = < 2.2e-16
bb <- pangmm(cigs ~ lag(cigs, 1) + price | lag(cigs, 2:99), data = g,
             index = c("id", "wave"), transformation = "ld",
             model = "twostep", collapse = TRUE, maxlag = 4)
summary(bb)
#> 
#> Call:
#> pangmm(formula = cigs ~ lag(cigs, 1) + price | lag(cigs, 2:99), 
#>     data = g, index = c("id", "wave"), transformation = "ld", 
#>     model = "twostep", collapse = TRUE, maxlag = 4)
#> 
#> Estimator: two-way two-step system GMM (Blundell-Bond) 
#> N = 300  T = 7  equations used = 3300  instruments = 12  vcov: robust (Windmeijer) 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> lag(cigs, 1)  0.50920    0.03825  13.313   <2e-16 ***
#> price        -0.26263    0.02786  -9.428   <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Arellano-Bond AR(1) test: z = -8.576, p = < 2.2e-16
#> Arellano-Bond AR(2) test: z = -1.041, p = 0.2978
#> Sargan test (not robust): chi2(4) = 5.905, p = 0.2064
#> Hansen J test (robust): chi2(4) = 4.635, p = 0.3269
#> Wald test for coefficients: chi2(2) = 268.8, p = < 2.2e-16

Both estimates are close to 0.5. The diagnostics to read are the Arellano-Bond tests, where AR(1) in the differenced residuals is expected and AR(2) must not be rejected (p = 0.34), and the Hansen test of the overidentifying restrictions. The two-step standard errors use the Windmeijer (2005) correction.

Finite-sample bias. GMM is consistent as the number of individuals grows, but in moderate samples it can be badly biased, and matching another package does not protect against it. Too many instruments overfit the endogenous regressor and pull the estimate toward pooled OLS, while making the Hansen test look too good (Roodman 2009). When the variance of the individual effect is large, the level moments of system GMM become weak (Bun and Windmeijer 2010). Practical rules:

  • prefer the two-step estimator;
  • use collapse = TRUE and a small maxlag, so that the instrument count stays well below the number of individuals (pangmm() warns when it does not; the uncollapsed fit above already uses 21 instruments with only 7 waves);
  • treat a Hansen p-value close to 1 (0.96 above) as a warning sign, not as support;
  • check that the persistence estimate lies between the fixed-effects (biased down) and pooled OLS (biased up) estimates (Bond 2002).

panglm() does not create panel lags in its formula, so build the lagged outcome first for the bounds.

g$cigs_lag <- ave(g$cigs, g$id, FUN = function(v) c(NA, head(v, -1)))
gl <- g[!is.na(g$cigs_lag), ]
ols <- panglm(cigs ~ cigs_lag + price, data = gl, index = c("id", "wave"),
              model = "pooling")
fe <- panglm(cigs ~ cigs_lag + price, data = gl, index = c("id", "wave"),
             model = "within")
c(fixed_effects = coef(fe)[["cigs_lag"]],
  difference_gmm = coef(ab)[["lag(cigs, 1)"]],
  system_gmm = coef(bb)[["lag(cigs, 1)"]],
  pooled_ols = coef(ols)[["cigs_lag"]])
#>  fixed_effects difference_gmm     system_gmm     pooled_ols 
#>      0.2311729      0.5502465      0.5091996      0.8431146

Both GMM estimates fall inside the bounds.

Sample selection

In a cohort, quality of life is observed only for patients who answer the questionnaire. If the health shock that lowers the score also makes patients less likely to respond, the respondents are a selected sample and fixed effects on them is biased. The correction of Wooldridge (1995) fits a probit of response for each wave, with the Mundlak means of the selection regressors, and adds the inverse Mills ratios, interacted with the wave, to the fixed-effects outcome equation. A variable that affects response but not the outcome (here a reminder letter) is needed for credible identification.

set.seed(1)
N <- 300; TT <- 4
s <- data.frame(id = rep(seq_len(N), each = TT), wave = rep(seq_len(TT), N))
alpha <- rep(rnorm(N), each = TT)
s$treat <- rnorm(N * TT) + 0.5 * alpha
s$reminder <- rnorm(N * TT)
v <- rnorm(N * TT)
u <- 0.7 * v + rnorm(N * TT, sd = 0.7)
s$respond <- as.numeric(0.3 + 0.5 * s$treat + s$reminder + 0.3 * alpha +
                          v > 0)
s$qol <- ifelse(s$respond == 1, 1 + 0.5 * s$treat + alpha + u, NA)

The standard errors come from a panel bootstrap that re-estimates both steps; 49 replicates keep this example fast, use at least 499 in practice.

coef(panglm(qol ~ treat, data = s[s$respond == 1, ],
            index = c("id", "wave"), model = "within"))
#>     treat 
#> 0.3537671
sel <- panselect(respond ~ treat + reminder, qol ~ treat, data = s,
                 index = c("id", "wave"), model = "within",
                 boot = 49, seed = 2)
summary(sel)
#> 
#> Call:
#> panselect(selection = respond ~ treat + reminder, outcome = qol ~ 
#>     treat, data = s, index = c("id", "wave"), model = "within", 
#>     boot = 49, seed = 2)
#> 
#> Wooldridge (1995) panel selection correction: fixed effects with Mundlak means, inverse Mills ratio by period 
#> Selection sample: N = 1200  groups = 300 
#> Outcome sample:   N = 710  groups = 286 
#> Probits fitted for periods: 1, 2, 3, 4 
#> 
#> Outcome equation (vcov: panel bootstrap, 49 replicates):
#>          Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> treat     0.45225    0.05037   8.978  < 2e-16 ***
#> lambda:1  0.98046    0.18266   5.368 7.98e-08 ***
#> lambda:2  0.76097    0.17850   4.263 2.02e-05 ***
#> lambda:3  0.80668    0.21728   3.713 0.000205 ***
#> lambda:4  0.81105    0.17365   4.671 3.00e-06 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Test of selection bias (H0: all inverse Mills ratio coefficients are zero):
#>   cluster-robust Wald chi2(4) = 56.2, p = 1.818e-11
#>   bootstrap Wald chi2(4) = 44.06, p = 6.232e-09
#> Residual df: 419

Fixed effects on the respondents gives 0.35 against a true 0.5. The corrected estimate is 0.45, and the joint test that all inverse Mills ratio coefficients are zero rejects clearly, so selection on the time-varying shock matters here. The test uses the cluster-robust covariance, which is valid under its null hypothesis; the coefficient standard errors use the bootstrap, which accounts for the first step.

Validated against

Fixed-effects, random-effects and pooled 2SLS reproduce plm::plm(), AER::ivreg() and fixest::feols(); Hausman-Taylor reproduces plm::pht(); difference and system GMM, including collapsed instruments, the Windmeijer correction and the Arellano-Bond, Sargan and Hansen tests, reproduce plm::pgmm(). No R package implements the Wooldridge (1995) panel correction, so panselect() is validated step by step: the probits against stats::glm(), the outcome equation against plm, the covariance against sandwich, and the one-period case against sampleSelection::heckit(). The scripts are in tests/testthat and validation/.

References

Balestra, P., and Varadharajan-Krishnakumar, J. (1987). Full information estimations of a system of simultaneous equations with error component structure. Econometric Theory, 3, 223-246.

Baltagi, B. H. (1981). Simultaneous equations with error components. Journal of Econometrics, 17, 189-200.

Blundell, R., and Bond, S. (1998). Initial conditions and moment restrictions in dynamic panel data models. Journal of Econometrics, 87, 115-143.

Bond, S. (2002). Dynamic panel data models: a guide to micro data methods and practice. Portuguese Economic Journal, 1, 141-162.

Bun, M. J. G., and Windmeijer, F. (2010). The weak instrument problem of the system GMM estimator in dynamic panel data models. The Econometrics Journal, 13, 95-126.

Hausman, J. A., and Taylor, W. E. (1981). Panel data and unobservable individual effects. Econometrica, 49, 1377-1398.

Nickell, S. (1981). Biases in dynamic models with fixed effects. Econometrica, 49, 1417-1426.

Roodman, D. (2009). How to do xtabond2: an introduction to difference and system GMM in Stata. Stata Journal, 9, 86-136.

Windmeijer, F. (2005). A finite sample correction for the variance of linear efficient two-step GMM estimators. Journal of Econometrics, 126, 25-51.

Wooldridge, J. M. (1995). Selection corrections for panel data models under conditional mean independence assumptions. Journal of Econometrics, 68, 115-132.
